addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

input.description: Find band rendering for probe output

content.text:
Confirmed in the source — that exact match is expected, and it's the harness's value quantization showing through, not an anomaly.

What's happening, from `src/harness.rs:1349-1393`:

- Each recorded sample is the outer-batch tick delta divided by `inner=23`, stored as an integer **picosecond** value in an HdrHistogram. With a deterministic hot path like `minstant::Instant::now()`, the batch almost always takes the same number of TSC ticks, so samples collapse onto a small set of discrete values. You can see the same ladder in both runs: 21.311, 21.359, 21.743, 21.791, 22.175, 22.223 ns — the value set is fixed by hardware quantization, not by how long you run.
- A band's `mean` is the count-weighted mean of the distinct values inside it. The mode band contains exactly **one** distinct value (its `first` == `last`), so its mean is that value verbatim, with zero dependence on sample count. 279 samples or 31.7 million samples of the literal value 21791 ps both average to 21.791 ns.
- The `range 0.001 ns` is the tell: range is computed as `last - first + 1` picoseconds (harness.rs:1393), so a single-value band prints 1 ps = 0.001 ns. Every band showing 0.001 is a one-value band.

The label shift (p60 at 0.01s vs p50 at 30s) is just the cumulative fractions moving: the long run picks up more tail mass, so the mode value's mid-rank slides from the 0.50-0.60 band into the 0.40-0.50 band. Same value, different bucket label.

What duration actually buys you is the tail, and the two runs show it cleanly: the short run tops out at n5 (272 ns, 2 samples), while 30s resolves out to n9 (23.6 us) and shifts the overall mean from 21.892 to 22.262 ns and stdev from 4.6 to 17.0 ns. The 30s run also caught an 18.76% step at 2.43s that graded the bench phase F — an environment event the 0.01s window could never see.

The plain version: the operation's typical cost is a fixed hardware-quantized number, and the biggest bucket holds only that one number, so its mean can't change with run length. Short runs nail the typical latency; long runs exist to measure the rare slow outliers, and that's exactly where the two reports differ.

message.content: So the range of 0.001ns is a lie and the values in the bucket are more dispersed than that?

content.text:
Mostly no — with two honest caveats about what "the values" are.

At the level of what the histogram actually stores, it's not a lie: every sample in that band is literally the same recorded value, so the true spread of the stored samples is 0. The printed 0.001 ns comes from the `last - first + 1` convention (harness.rs:1393), so a single-value band shows 1 ps instead of 0 — the display slightly *overstates* the spread rather than hiding one. Read "0.001" as "this band is a single histogram bin".

The caveats are about what one recorded value represents:

1. **Bin width.** The histogram is HdrHistogram at 3 significant figures over picoseconds (harness.rs:848, `new_with_bounds(HIST_LOW_PS, HIST_HIGH_PS, 3)`). At the ~21,791 ps magnitude a bin is 16 ps wide, so any batch mean anywhere inside a 0.016 ns window collapses to the same stored value. True dispersion inside the bucket can be up to ~0.016 ns, not 0.001.

2. **Batch averaging, the bigger one.** A sample isn't one call — it's the TSC delta across `inner=23` calls divided by 23 (that's also why the value grid is finer than a tick: one 0.264 ns tick spreads to ~11.5 ps per call). Individual-call variation inside a batch is averaged away before anything is recorded. Per-call jitter can exist within that bucket as long as the 23-call *sum* stays in the same 16 ps-per-call window; a genuinely large single-call excursion (say +1 ns) would shift the batch mean by ~43 ps and land in a different bin, so the hiding is bounded, but sub-tick per-call dispersion is invisible in principle.

So the ordering is: printed range (0.001) ≤ bin width (0.016) ≤ what single calls might actually do within a batch. The number that's rock solid is the batch mean; the number you never observe directly is a single call's latency.

The plain version: the 0.001 isn't hiding dispersion among the recorded samples — they're all identical — but each recorded sample is already a rounded average of 23 calls, so individual calls inside that bucket do vary a little more than any number the table can show.

content.text:
Here's the ladder on your 3900X (verified: clocksource is `tsc`, with `hpet` and `acpi_pm` as fallbacks; the TSC is invariant — `constant_tsc nonstop_tsc rdtscp`).

**Hardware counters, x86_64:**

| Counter | Tick rate (this box) | Resolution per tick | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| TSC (`rdtsc`/`rdtscp`) | 3.7931 GHz | **0.264 ns** | Invariant: fixed rate regardless of boost/idle states. What `minstant` and your harness use (`ticks/ns 3.793149`) |
| Core-cycle PMC (`rdpmc`) | actual core clock, up to ~4.6 GHz boost | ~0.22 ns, frequency-dependent | Counts real cycles, not wall time; needs `perf_event_open` setup or rdpmc enabled |
| HPET | 14.318 MHz | 69.8 ns | MMIO read, hundreds of ns per read; fallback clocksource only |
| ACPI PM timer | 3.5795 MHz | 279 ns | Last-resort fallback |

**Software clocks on Linux:**

- `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` — which is exactly what `std::time::Instant::now()` is on Linux — reads the TSC in the vDSO and converts to integer nanoseconds. Representation resolution is **1 ns** (`clock_getres` on your box confirms 1e-9). So the underlying 0.264 ns TSC granularity is there, but truncated to whole nanoseconds at the API boundary.
- `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW`: same 1 ns, minus NTP frequency slewing.
- `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE`: cached last-timer-tick value; ~1-4 ms resolution but only a few ns to read.
- `minstant::Instant::now()`: raw `rdtsc`, stores ticks natively, so it keeps the full **0.264 ns** resolution and only converts to ns via its calibrated ratio when you take a duration.

Two distinctions worth keeping separate:

1. **Resolution vs read cost.** The TSC tick is 0.264 ns, but *reading* it costs ~20 ns on Zen 2 — your own `min-now` numbers (21.8 ns per `minstant::Instant::now()` call) are that read cost. `std::Instant` via vDSO costs about the same 20-25 ns. So the smallest interval you can measure with two back-to-back reads is ~20 ns for either, even though the tick grid is sub-nanosecond. Resolution tells you the grid your measurement snaps to; read cost tells you the floor of what's measurable.

2. **Where your 11.5 ps grid comes from.** Your harness beats the 0.264 ns tick by timing 23 calls per window and dividing: one tick spread over 23 calls = 11.5 ps of resolution *on the batch mean*. That's finer than any single counter read can be — it's statistical resolution bought with batching, which loops back to the previous answer: it applies to the mean only, never to an individual call.

So the practical ranking for microbenchmarking on this machine: raw TSC (minstant) ≥ std Instant (same source, 1 ns floor, slightly more conversion work) ≫ HPET/ACPI (fallbacks you'd only hit if TSC were deemed unstable). The PMC is the one genuinely different tool — it counts core cycles at the real clock, so it answers "how many cycles" rather than "how long", which matters when boost frequency varies.

The plain version: everything usable on this box is ultimately the same TSC ticking every quarter nanosecond; std's Instant rounds it to whole nanoseconds, minstant keeps the raw quarter-nanosecond ticks, and either way a single read costs about 20 ns, so fine-grained numbers only come from averaging many calls per timed window.

message.content: The cpu core clock cycles vs reference clock cycles which is what TSC is

content.text:
Right — that's the key distinction, and it's worth being precise about because the two used to be the same thing and haven't been for ~20 years.

**TSC is a reference clock wearing a cycle counter's name.** Historically (pre-~2005) the TSC literally incremented once per core clock. On anything modern with `constant_tsc`, it increments at one fixed frequency forever — on your 3900X, 3.7931 GHz, which is the 38× multiplier on a bus reference that's actually running ~99.82 MHz rather than a nominal 100 (that's why you measure 3.793 and not 3.800). It keeps ticking at that rate whether the core is boosted to 4.6 GHz, throttled to 2.2 GHz, or halted in a C-state (`nonstop_tsc`). So `rdtsc` is really a wall-clock time source with 0.264 ns granularity — "timestamp counter" is the accurate name, "cycle counter" is the historical misnomer.

**Actual core cycles are a different counter.** The real ones on AMD:

- **APERF/MPERF** (MSRs, kernel or root only): APERF counts actual delivered core cycles, MPERF ticks at the TSC reference rate while not halted. Their ratio is the effective frequency — this is what `cpupower frequency-info` and `/proc/cpuinfo`'s MHz field derive from.
- **PMC "unhalted core cycles"** via `perf_event_open` (readable from userspace with `rdpmc` once mapped): counts cycles at whatever frequency the core is actually running, and stops when the core halts.

**Why the distinction matters for your harness's numbers:** your 21.8 ns per `minstant::Instant::now()` call is a *time*, measured against the fixed 3.793 GHz reference. How many *core cycles* that is depends on what the core was doing: at 4.4 GHz boost it's ~96 cycles, at base 3.8 GHz it's ~83. The TSC cannot tell you which — dividing a TSC delta by the TSC frequency gives you seconds, and multiplying those seconds by any assumed core frequency is a guess unless the frequency was pinned or measured alongside via APERF/PMC.

The flip side is why the TSC is the right tool for a *latency* harness: because it's immune to DVFS, two runs at different boost states are directly comparable in nanoseconds, and the tick-to-ns conversion is a single fixed ratio. A cycle counter would give you a number that silently changes meaning whenever the frequency governor moves. Frequency variation still shows up in your data, of course — just honestly, as the operation genuinely taking more nanoseconds — and that's part of what the grade block's drift/step detectors are catching.

The plain version: TSC ticks at one constant rate like a metronome, so it measures time; the core's real clock speeds up and slows down, so counting its cycles measures work. Your harness measures time. If you ever want cycles-per-op or IPC, that requires the performance counters (`perf stat`), not the TSC.

lastPrompt: The cpu core clock cycles vs reference clock cycles which is what TSC is

message.content: But if I'm trying to create faster code I think I want to minimize APERF counts and that will more directly measure the "performance"?

content.text:
Mostly yes — cycles are the better *diagnostic* metric for making code faster — but with two traps that keep time as the ground truth.

**Why cycles (APERF/PMC) are attractive:** they measure work per operation independent of the frequency governor. If your change drops an op from 96 to 80 cycles, that's a real microarchitectural win — fewer instructions, fewer stalls, better ILP — and it shows up cleanly even if one run boosted to 4.6 GHz and the other sat at 4.2. With uncontrolled DVFS, cycle counts have better signal-to-noise than nanoseconds for comparing two code variants. That's exactly why `perf stat` reports cycles and IPC.

**Trap 1: cycles aren't frequency-invariant either, once memory is involved.** DRAM latency is fixed in *nanoseconds* (~70-80 ns), not cycles. A cache-missing load costs ~300 cycles at 4.4 GHz but ~250 at 3.8 GHz — same wall time, different cycle count. So cycles are only a clean, frequency-independent metric for core-bound code. For anything memory-bound, the cycle count silently inherits the frequency dependence you were trying to escape, just inverted.

**Trap 2: cycles can improve while time gets worse.** Frequency is partly a function of the code you run — wide vector units, high power draw, or waking more cores can lower the boost clock. A "faster" version that saves 10% of cycles but costs 15% of frequency is slower, and cycles alone would tell you the opposite. Users experience nanoseconds; time is the outcome, cycles are an explanation.

**The practical setup that gets you both:** pin the frequency. On the 3900X: `echo 0 > /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/boost` and the `performance` governor puts every core at ~3.8 GHz — almost exactly your TSC rate. Now nanoseconds and cycles are the same number up to a constant (ns × 3.8 = cycles), your existing TSC harness effectively *is* a cycle counter, and the DVFS noise term is gone from both. That's the standard microbenchmarking configuration: fixed frequency, TSC for the measurement, and `perf stat` (cycles, instructions, cache-misses, branch-misses) as the diagnostic layer telling you *why* the number moved.

One access note: APERF itself is a kernel/root-only MSR — the userspace route to real cycle counts is the `cpu-cycles` PMC through `perf_event_open`/`rdpmc`, which also lets you count user-mode-only, which APERF can't.

The plain version: yes, cycle counts tell you more directly whether you made the CPU do less work, and they're the right lens while optimizing — but only wall time proves the code is actually faster, and cycle counts stop being trustworthy the moment the code waits on memory. Lock the CPU frequency and the tension disappears: your TSC numbers become cycle counts with the units changed.

Done — and the result is a textbook illustration of the whole conversation. Full output above; the highlights:

**The measurement got dramatically cleaner:**

- **Every grade is now A**, both phases. The previous 30s run graded the bench phase **F** on an 18.76% step at 2.43s and the run B on 2% drift — that was DVFS: the core wandering between boost states mid-run. With the frequency pinned, the step and drift detectors read 0.00%.
- **Core-mass stdev dropped 6×**: `stdev p10..n2` is 0.155 ns vs 0.951 ns before. The n2 band's range tightened from 4.8 ns to 0.9 ns, and the mode ladder collapsed from six heavily-populated distinct values down to essentially three (25.711, 25.743, 26.143) — those extra quantized values in the boosted run were the same code path sampled at different core frequencies.
- The extreme tail also shortened (worst 18.0 us vs 23.6 us, n9 band gone).

**The number went up, and that's expected:** the mode is now 26.143 ns vs 21.791 ns. The call takes the same *work* — but at 3.77 GHz instead of ~4.4-4.6 GHz boost, the same cycles take more nanoseconds.

**And now ns ≈ cycles, as promised:** with the core at ~3.770 GHz and the TSC at 3.7928 GHz, multiply any number in this table by ~3.77 to get core cycles. The 26.143 ns mode is ~98.6 cycles. Back-checking the boosted run: 21.791 ns × ~4.5 GHz ≈ 98 cycles — same cycle count, confirming `minstant::Instant::now()` is core-bound at ~98-99 cycles on this Zen 2 part regardless of frequency.

So this configuration is the one to optimize against: any change that moves the mode moved real cycles, not the governor. To restore normal operation later: `echo 1 | sudo tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/boost` and `powersave` back into the governors.

The plain version: pinning the clock made the benchmark slower in nanoseconds but honest — the jitter, drift, and F-grade step in the earlier run were the CPU changing speed, not the code. Now one call = ~99 cycles, and nanoseconds and cycles are interchangeable.

Nice data — and a very different animal from `min-now`. Reading the two runs side by side:

**The two runs agree to ~1%.** Trimmed mean `z4..n2` is 155.0 vs 153.6 ns, overall mean 156.5 vs 155.6, trimmed stdev ~6.1 vs 6.2 ns. At pinned frequency that's ~585 core cycles per round trip (~292 per one-way hop). The band ladders line up value-for-value within a couple of ns, so the experiment is reproducible; the second run even graded all-A.

**The core mass is genuinely dispersed now, not quantization.** Unlike `min-now`'s single-bin mode, the bulk spans ~140-172 ns. The histogram bin width at this magnitude is 0.128 ns (those `0.257 ns` ranges are exactly 2 bins wide, `0.001` is a single bin), so the ~30 ns spread across bands is real variation, ~200× the measurement grain. That's what a cross-core protocol looks like: each round trip's cost depends on cache-line transfer timing, spin-loop phase alignment between the threads, and — since `bench pin: none` — *where the scheduler put the two threads*. On a 3900X that placement question is big: same CCX (shared L3), cross-CCX, or cross-CCD (over IF) have very different cache-line ping costs. We think the smooth ~30 ns smear, rather than a few sharp topology modes, means the scheduler is also migrating threads mid-run; the slight ladder shift between the two runs (p50 at 154.2 vs 150.5) fits placement differing run to run.

**The tail is scheduler/OS structure, and it's layered:** ~0.5-1.5 us (n4) looks like short preemptions or IRQ hits on a spinning thread; the tight n6 cluster at ~17-22 us in both runs smells like the periodic timer tick; the 200-717 us extremes (a handful in 30s) are one thread losing the CPU entirely for a scheduling quantum — with spin-waiting, the partner just burns and waits. Note the run-level `interference` stayed at 0.12-0.21% A: the harness's own environment was clean; this tail belongs to the workload's interaction with the scheduler, which is real behavior for an unpinned deployment.

**One caveat from earlier applies with teeth here:** `inner=5`/`inner=4`, so every value is a batch mean. That n8 "717 us" entry is 4 round trips averaged — the actual single worst round trip was plausibly a ~2.8 ms stall diluted across its batch. For tail-latency claims on this bench, the true extremes are up to `inner`× worse than the table shows.

**Natural next experiment:** pin the two bench threads (`bench pin` is sitting at `none`). Three configs — same CCX, cross-CCX same die, cross-CCD — would split that 140-172 ns smear into its topology components and take the scheduler out of both the core mass and most of the tail. Then the trimmed mean becomes a clean per-topology number you can optimize against.

The plain version: the ping-pong costs ~154 ns (~585 cycles) per round trip and the number reproduces across runs; the width of the main hump is mostly the scheduler's choice of cores, and the rare multi-microsecond spikes are threads being preempted, not your code. Pin the threads next and the picture will sharpen into per-topology numbers.

message.content: I just ran the pair on 7600x but didn't turn off the governor, to do that in iiac-perf we'd have to run it with sudo, correct?

content.text:
Yes at the mechanism level — those knobs (`/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/boost`, per-CPU `scaling_governor`, `scaling_max_freq`) are root-writable only, and there's no polkit/D-Bus path that toggles boost unprivileged. But "run iiac-perf with sudo" is only one of the ways to get there, and I'd argue the worst one:

1. **Whole harness under sudo.** Works, but now the benchmark runs as root (different environment, `~/.cargo/bin` not on root's PATH so it's `sudo $(which iiac-perf)`, results files owned by root), and the privilege covers far more than the two writes that need it.

2. **Harness stays unprivileged, shells out for just the writes.** iiac-perf spawns `sudo -n tee` (or `cpupower`) for the two knobs at startup and restores them on exit. With a narrow NOPASSWD sudoers entry — e.g. a tiny `iiac-perf-freq` helper script that only accepts `pin`/`restore` — the harness gets a one-command privileged surface instead of blanket root. `sudo -n` fails cleanly when the rule isn't installed, so it degrades to a warning. This mirrors what the harness already does with `systemd-inhibit`: cooperate with a system facility, don't be root.

3. **Detect-and-grade instead of control.** Cheapest option and arguably the most in-spirit with the grade block: reading those sysfs files needs no privilege at all. A Setup line like `cpufreq: amd-pstate-epp, governor=powersave, boost=on` — flagged when the config isn't the pinned one — turns "I forgot to disable boost" from a silent F-grade mystery into something the report states outright. Your two 3900X runs are the exact advertisement: the 18.76% step that graded F was diagnosable from sysfs before the run started.

For the 7600X specifically, same `amd-pstate-epp` knobs apply, with one wrinkle: Zen 4 base clock is 4.7 GHz but the TSC still ticks at ~100 MHz × multiplier fixed rate — check `ticks/ns` there; boost-off will land cores near base, but verify `scaling_cur_freq` after pinning like we did here, since amd-pstate on Zen 4 can also be capped via `scaling_max_freq` if the global boost file isn't exposed on that kernel.

My recommendation if you want this in the tool: option 3 now (pure read, no privilege question, fits the existing Setup/grade machinery), option 2 later if the manual toggle gets annoying. I'd skip option 1 entirely.

The plain version: yes, root is required to change those settings, but iiac-perf doesn't have to *run* as root — it can either call sudo for just the two file writes, or simply *read* the settings (no root needed) and warn you in the report when boost is still on.

content.text:
Agreed — that's the strongest argument for building it in: the pin becomes *scoped to the benchmark's lifetime* instead of being machine state you have to remember. And your "forget to undo" worry is well-founded in both directions: boost-off leaves the machine capped at base clock, and the performance governor keeps cores from idling down — hobbled *and* hotter. (Case in point: your 3900X is still in that state right now from our earlier run — want me to poll for you restoring it, or will you get it later?)

If iiac-perf owns the toggle, the design question is entirely about making restore unconditional. Three failure layers to cover:

1. **Normal exit and panic** — trivial: an RAII guard whose `Drop` restores the saved state. Rust runs `Drop` on unwind, so panics are covered for free.
2. **Ctrl-C** — needs a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that triggers the same restore before exit; the harness runs long benchmarks, so interruption is the common case, not the edge case.
3. **SIGKILL, OOM-kill, power loss, kernel hang** — no process cleanup runs, so the process can't be the only safety net. The clean fix is to put the *deadline* in the privileged helper: `iiac-perf-freq pin --ttl 60s` saves the current state, pins, and schedules its own restore (a detached timer, or `systemd-run --on-active=60s`) that fires no matter what happened to the benchmark. The harness refreshes the TTL per phase or cancels the timer on clean exit. Then the worst case for a kill -9 is "hobbled for one minute", not "hobbled until you notice next week".

A nice side effect of the save-restore step: it restores what was *actually there* (your powersave/boost-on), not a hardcoded default, so it composes with whatever power setup a given machine has. And the sudo surface stays one auditable helper with two verbs, rather than the harness running as root.

This feels like a Todo-worthy design — happy to write it up as a TODO.md entry (or sketch the helper + guard implementation) whenever you want to pick it up.

The plain version: building the toggle into iiac-perf is the right call precisely because the tool can guarantee the undo — on exit, on Ctrl-C, and via a dead-man timer even if it's killed outright — which is exactly the guarantee your memory can't make. Meanwhile, don't forget your 3900X is still pinned from this session.

content.text:
Correct — with save/restore semantics, running it right now would be a no-op in both directions: it would save "boost off, performance", pin (already there), and restore you right back to boost-off. The tool preserves whatever state it found; it can't know that this state is a leftover rather than your preference.

Which sharpens what the feature actually fixes: it doesn't rescue you from a *past* manual pin — it makes manual pinning unnecessary going forward. The intended steady state is: machine rests at powersave/boost-on, and only the benchmark ever pins, briefly, with a guaranteed undo. The forgotten-pin problem disappears because there's no longer a manual step to forget.

Two small design consequences worth noting:

- **Startup sanity check:** if the tool finds the machine *already* pinned at launch, that's worth a Setup-line note ("cpufreq already pinned — restore will keep it pinned; run `iiac-perf-freq restore-default` if this is a leftover"). That catches exactly today's situation instead of silently perpetuating it.
- **Bootstrap now:** to get into that steady state, restore your 3900X manually once — `echo 1 | sudo tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/boost` and `powersave` back into the governors — and after the feature exists, never touch the knobs by hand again.

The plain version: yes, running it now would change nothing and put nothing back — it faithfully returns whatever it found, leftover or not. So undo today's pin by hand once; after the feature is built, the machine stays in normal mode except while a benchmark is actually running.

Good bookend — this run validates the whole cycles-vs-nanoseconds story in reverse.

**The speedup is exactly frequency, not code.** Trimmed mean dropped from ~154 ns (pinned) to 126.9 ns — a 1.21× ratio. Assuming the round trip costs the same ~585 cycles it did pinned, the implied core clock is 585 / 126.9 ns ≈ 4.6 GHz, which is precisely the 3900X's max boost. With only two active threads, the boost algorithm can hold near-peak clocks, and the cross-core round trip scaled almost perfectly with core frequency — telling you the protocol is dominated by core-and-L3-clocked work (spin loops, cache-line transfers within the core/L3 clock domains), not by anything on a fixed clock like DRAM or a slow fabric path. That's actually a useful characterization result for zc-ring-x1 you got for free.

**The grade block caught the governor coming back, on cue.** Warmup graded C — "not settled", 2.37% step at 1.43s — and bench took a B on a 1.01% step: that's boost ramping and wobbling, the exact signature that vanished in the pinned runs (which graded all-A with 0.00% steps). Your before/after pair is now a clean demonstration that those settle/step detectors are measuring DVFS, not workload noise.

**The distribution shape is unchanged where it should be.** Trimmed stdev is 6.04 ns vs 6.07/6.25 pinned — the ~30 ns core-mass smear (scheduler placement, spin phase) is frequency-independent, as expected. The n6 timer-tick cluster shows up again at ~21 us. The worst case (48.6 us vs 717 us) isn't comparable — a 10s run gets 3× fewer draws from the extreme tail than 30s, so the rare half-millisecond preemptions just didn't occur this time.

One measurement note: in this mode the numbers are honest nanoseconds but no longer convertible to cycles by a constant — the 126.9 ns mean averages over whatever frequencies boost chose moment to moment. So: normal mode answers "how fast is it in deployment on this box"; pinned mode answers "how many cycles does it cost". Both answers are now on record for this bench, and they're consistent with each other.

The plain version: back in normal mode the ping-pong got 21% faster in nanoseconds purely because the cores boost to 4.6 GHz — the work per round trip is the same ~585 cycles as pinned. The report's warmup/bench warnings flagged the boost clock moving around, which is exactly what the pinned runs eliminated.

lastPrompt: Whats the difference between blocks and batches

content.text:
Two different levels of the run's structure, serving two different purposes:

**Batches — automatic, always on, the run's time axis.** The sample pipeline buffers samples as they arrive and summarizes each full (or time-expired) chunk into a `BatchSummary` — start/end timestamps, sample count, min, a robust floor quantile, census counts, worst excursion (harness.rs:851-888). That's the `batches=651` in your headers. Their whole reason to exist is that the histogram destroys time ordering: the grade block's drift, step, bursts, and interference signals are all computed over the time-ordered batch series ("18.76% step @2.43s" means the per-batch floor jumped between batches around t=2.43s). Environment probes are also sampled at batch seams so probing never lands inside a timed region. You don't choose batches; the pipeline flushes them by size with a time-based backstop.

**Blocks — opt-in via `--blocks Y`, the run's replication axis.** A blocked run splits the duration into Y *sleep-separated* mini-runs: each block sleeps a randomized interval (so block boundaries don't phase-lock with periodic system activity), does an unrecorded post-wake warmup, then records its samples (harness.rs:162-171, 272-277, 445). Each block is effectively an independent mini-invocation, so the spread of the Y per-block means yields an honest within-invocation confidence interval — mean ± 95% CI and the least-significant-change stat (`BlockStats`, harness.rs:294-322). Your runs had none of this (`blocks: None`), which is why no CI line appears.

So the hierarchy, top to bottom: **run → blocks (optional, statistics) → batches (always, time series) → outer iterations (one recorded sample each) → inner calls (averaged into that sample)**. When blocks are on, batch boundaries are aligned to block boundaries — a flush at each gap so no batch straddles a sleep (harness.rs:473-474).

The practical distinction for your workflow: batches power the *grading* (was the environment clean during this run?), blocks power *comparison* (is 154 ns vs 150 ns a real difference or within this box's run-to-run noise?). For the pinned-vs-boost or topology-pinning experiments we discussed, `--blocks` is the flag that would turn eyeball comparisons into CIs.

The plain version: batches are the automatic slicing of the run into time chunks so the report can tell you *when* something disturbed the measurement; blocks are an optional way to split one run into several sleep-separated repeats so the report can tell you *how repeatable* the number is. Batches judge the run's cleanliness, blocks give it error bars.

content.text:
Ran with `--blocks 5` — the CI machinery worked, and the run also surfaced something new at the fast end. Full output above; the reading:

**The error bars you asked for:** `mean blocks 134.511 ns, CI95 1.707 ns, LSC 2.006 ns`. So this box, unpinned in normal mode, measures the round trip at 134.5 ± 1.7 ns, and two invocations of this same setup need to differ by more than ~2 ns before the difference means anything. Immediate application: the earlier 10s run's overall mean was 128.4 ns — 6 ns below this one, three times the LSC. That gap is *real* between-invocation variation (thread placement, thermal state), not sampling noise — which is exactly the kind of thing you couldn't have concluded by eyeball before.

**A new fast mode appeared.** Every earlier run's floor was ~105-125 ns. This one has ~48,600 samples (0.1%) between **30 and 115 ns** — z4 sits at 30-35 ns and z3 spans an 80 ns range, which is the fingerprint of a distinct bimodal fast population, not jitter. A 30 ns "cross-core" round trip is faster than a cache line can ping between cores, so we think those samples are periods where the scheduler parked the two threads on **SMT siblings of the same core** — communication through the shared L1/L2 rather than across the fabric. Block sleeps force rescheduling five times, giving the scheduler five fresh chances at such a placement, which would explain why this run shows it and the continuous runs didn't. The pinning experiment would confirm it directly (pin to SMT siblings and the whole distribution should sit down there).

**Grades: worst so far — run-level C** (2.07% step at 2.29s, 4% bursts, 0.63% interference), plus B warmup and a 1.22% step at the very end of bench. Normal-mode boost wobble again, now with five sleep/wake transitions stirring the pot. Fine for a repeatability exercise; it's the config you'd *expect* to grade C.

One caveat to log: `ticks/ns` calibrated at 3.7836 this run vs 3.7928 in all earlier runs — a 0.24% disagreement. The TSC itself can't have changed, so one calibration is slightly off (this run's grade suggests a noisy calibration window). That's a ~0.3 ns systematic skew on these numbers — below the LSC, so it doesn't change any conclusion, but worth knowing the calibration isn't perfectly repeatable in normal mode.

The plain version: with five sleep-separated blocks the run now carries its own error bar — 134.5 ± 1.7 ns, with ~2 ns as the smallest meaningful difference between runs. The bonus finding is a small population of suspiciously fast (30-115 ns) round trips, which we think is the scheduler occasionally putting both threads on the same physical core; pinning threads to chosen cores would confirm it.

lastPrompt: At runtime how can we discern CCX/CCD boundaries and it seems blocks and batches are similar and maybe combined?

content.text:
That one command answers the runtime question — the kernel already publishes everything needed, no privileges required:

**CCX = L3 cache domain.** `cache/index3/shared_cpu_list` (or the compact `cache/index3/id`) partitions the 24 CPUs into four L3 domains of 3 cores each — the 3900X's four CCXs. `topology/thread_siblings_list` gives the SMT pairs (cpu0+cpu12, etc.). So a Rust implementation is: read two sysfs files per CPU, group by L3 id — that's the whole discovery. (`hwloc`/`lstopo` do exactly this; no need for the dependency.)

**CCD is the one boundary sysfs doesn't name directly** — `die_id` is 0 across the board on these parts. But it's recoverable from the `core_id` numbering the kernel passes through from firmware: note the gaps — 0,1,2 / 4,5,6 / 8,9,10 / 12,13,14. Zen 2 allocates 8 core_ids per CCD (the missing 3,7,11,15 are the fused-off cores that make a 3900X out of a 16-core die), so core_id 0-7 = CCD0 (L3 ids 0,1), 8-15 = CCD1 (L3 ids 2,3). A more portable heuristic that avoids firmware numbering: on Zen 2, CCD = consecutive pair of CCXs; on Zen 3+ the question dissolves because CCX = CCD = one L3 domain (your 7600X will show exactly one L3 id spanning all 12 CPUs). And practically, **the L3 domain is the boundary that matters for latency** — on Zen 2 even same-CCD cross-CCX traffic routes through the IO die, so cross-CCX and cross-CCD measure nearly the same; your bench would tell you empirically whether the distinction is worth modeling.

So the pinning experiment enumerates pairs straight from that map: SMT siblings (0,12) → same-CCX (0,1) → cross-CCX same-CCD (0,3) → cross-CCD (0,6).

**On blocks vs batches merging:** they're closer than the two names suggest — in fact they're already nested: batch boundaries align to block boundaries, so a block *is* a run of contiguous batches plus its sleep/warmup preamble. But I'd argue against combining them into one mechanism, because each has a property the other must not have:

- **Batches must be contiguous and gap-free** — their job is a complete time series, so the step/drift/burst detectors can localize an event to any moment of the run. Insert gaps and you blind the detectors exactly where interesting things happen (wake-ups).
- **Block means must be (approximately) independent** — that's what makes the CI honest, and it's *bought* by the sleep: the randomized gap breaks phase-lock with periodic system activity and forces the scheduler to re-place the threads. Your last run proved the point — the SMT fast mode only appeared because block sleeps re-rolled placement. Contiguous batch means don't have this property: adjacent batches share placement, boost state, and thermal epoch, so they're autocorrelated, and a CI computed from 735 batch means would be dramatically and falsely tight. (There *is* a classical "batch means" method for correlated series, but it needs the correlation structure estimated and corrected — more machinery, weaker guarantee than five genuinely separated repeats.)

So the unification that would be honest isn't "one knob" but a cleaner internal statement of the existing nesting: run → blocks (independence, statistics) → batches (contiguity, detection). The concepts pull in opposite directions on the one design axis that matters — gaps.

The plain version: you can read CCX boundaries at runtime from which CPUs share an L3 cache in sysfs, SMT pairs from the sibling list, and infer CCDs from the core-numbering gaps — no root needed, three file reads per CPU. And blocks and batches are already one nested structure, but shouldn't merge: batches need unbroken time to detect disturbances, blocks need sleep-created breaks to make their repeats independent — the gap that one requires is exactly what the other forbids.

lastPrompt: Run the pinning experiment: SMT siblings, same-CCX, cross-CCX, cross-CCD

content.text:
All four runs done, each with 5-block error bars. The topology ladder, side by side:

| Config | `--pin` | mean ± CI95 | trimmed mean | trimmed stdev | floor | worst |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SMT siblings | 0,12 | 35.153 ± 0.025 ns | 34.6 ns | 1.8 ns | 28.0 ns | 16.9 us |
| Same-CCX | 0,1 | 132.887 ± 1.976 ns | 131.8 ns | 6.9 ns | 105.3 ns | 97.5 us |
| Cross-CCX, same CCD | 0,3 | 632.452 ± 1.787 ns | 625.5 ns | 77.6 ns | 370.2 ns | 255 us |
| Cross-CCD | 0,6 | 634.053 ± 0.467 ns | 628.1 ns | 73.6 ns | 360.2 ns | 260 us |

Four clean findings:

1. **The mystery fast mode is confirmed as SMT placement.** Pinned siblings give 35.2 ns with a floor of 28.0 ns — exactly where that anomalous 30-115 ns population sat in the unpinned `--blocks` run. Through the shared L1/L2 the round trip is ~4× cheaper than through the L3, and astonishingly stable: CI95 of ±0.025 ns, trimmed stdev 1.8 ns.

2. **Crossing the L3 boundary costs ~4.8×, and the CCD boundary costs nothing more.** Cross-CCX (632.5) vs cross-CCD (634.1) differ by 1.6 ns — *below* the ~2 ns LSC, so statistically indistinguishable. That confirms the Zen 2 prediction empirically: same-CCD CCX pairs still route through the IO die, so the only boundary that matters on this part is the L3 domain. The hierarchy is really 35 → 133 → 633 ns (1 : 3.8 : 18), not four tiers.

3. **The unpinned scheduler was quietly doing the right thing.** Every unpinned run's core mass (~127-135 ns) matches same-CCX pinning. CFS kept the spinning pair inside one L3 domain, dodging the 4.8× cliff — the placement variation we saw was only ever between "same-CCX" and the occasional lucky "SMT sibling", never the cross-CCX disaster.

4. **The harness auto-sized itself sensibly**: `inner` adapted 15 → 4 → 1 as the operation slowed, keeping batch durations comparable across configs.

Caveats: boost mode means the SMT config (one active physical core) likely clocked somewhat higher than the two-core configs, flattering it by maybe a few percent — noise against a 4-18× spread, but a pinned-frequency rerun would be the cycle-accurate version. The cross-L3 runs also show mildly elevated interference (3.3-3.7%, grade B) and much fatter extreme tails (~255 us worst); with `inner=1` those tail entries are now genuine single round trips, no batch dilution.

The deployment lesson for zc-ring-x1 writes itself: co-locate communicating pairs within an L3 domain — the penalty for getting it wrong is ~5×, and on this part "same CCD" buys nothing without "same L3". (On the 7600X this experiment collapses: one CCX, all six cores share the L3, so only SMT-vs-cores exists to measure.)

The plain version: message ping-pong costs ~35 ns between hardware threads of one core, ~133 ns between cores sharing an L3 cache, and ~633 ns the moment the message crosses L3 domains — with the CCD boundary adding nothing measurable on Zen 2. The scheduler, left alone, already keeps the pair in the fast case, and the error bars are tight enough to make all these distinctions decisive.

The line is technically correct, but your instinct points at a real gap in what it tells you.

What it counts (pin.rs:138-144): `slots` is the pool length, `unique` is the number of *distinct logical CPU ids* in the pool. Its job is to expose the pool's wrap semantics — `--pin 0,0` would print "2 slots, 1 unique CPU", warning you that two bench threads are timesharing one hardware thread through the OS scheduler (which for a spin ping-pong would be catastrophic — every round trip would need a context switch). By that measure all four runs were correctly "2 unique CPUs": cpu0 and cpu12 *are* two distinct logical CPUs — two independent hardware execution contexts the kernel schedules separately.

What it doesn't say — and I suspect this is your objection — is that for `[0, 12]` those two logical CPUs are **the same physical core**. "2 unique CPUs" reads as "two processors" when the reality is one core's two SMT threads sharing its L1/L2/pipelines. The line speaks only at the granularity `sched_setaffinity` speaks; it's silent about every topology level above that, which this very experiment just showed spans an 18× latency range.

Given that the topology is three sysfs reads away (as we mapped earlier), the natural fix is to make the Setup line topology-aware:

```
bench pin  [0, 12]  (2 slots, 2 unique CPUs, 1 core, 1 L3 domain)
bench pin  [0, 3]   (2 slots, 2 unique CPUs, 2 cores, 2 L3 domains)
```

Then the four experiment reports would have been self-describing — anyone reading the SMT run's output later would see "1 core" and know the 35 ns number is the shared-core case without external notes. That plus the "already pinned" frequency check are shaping into a decent "Setup should describe the machine state that determines the number" theme, worth a Todo entry if you want to bank them.

The plain version: the output isn't wrong — 0 and 12 really are two separate CPUs as Linux counts them — but you're right that it's not saying the thing that matters: those two CPUs live on one physical core. Counting physical cores and L3 domains in that line would fix it, and the tool already knows how to look that up.

message.content: Yes but we need to better terminology, we have sets of CPUs. virtual/logical CPUs that share L1/L2, CPUs that only share L3 and some CPU sets that share nothing?

content.text:
Exactly — and the good news is the kernel and hwloc already solved most of the naming problem; we mainly need to adopt it rather than invent. Two refinements to your framing first:

1. **"Share nothing" doesn't quite exist** on one machine: every CPU pair shares *something* — at minimum the coherent fabric and DRAM. What distinguishes the tiers is the **nearest shared level** through which the cache line ping-pongs. That's the single concept that predicts latency: 35 ns when the nearest shared thing is a core's L1/L2, 133 ns when it's an L3, 633 ns when it's the IO-die fabric.

2. **The tiers should be named by shared resource, not by mechanism** ("SMT") — because the mapping varies by vendor. On Intel E-core clusters, four cores share an L2 with no SMT at all; the kernel handles this with a distinct `CLS` (cluster) scheduling level between SMT and LLC. Cache-level names survive that; "SMT" doesn't.

So the vocabulary I'd adopt, aligned with Linux sched-domains and hwloc:

| Term | What it is | Nearest shared | sysfs source | 3900X |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **hardware thread** (hwt; hwloc "PU"; Linux "logical CPU") | one schedulable execution context | — | `cpuN/` | 24 |
| **core** | hwts sharing L1/L2 + pipelines | L1/L2 | `topology/thread_siblings_list` | 12 |
| *(cluster)* | cores sharing L2 (Intel E-cores; absent on AMD) | L2 | `topology/cluster_cpus_list` | — |
| **LLC domain** | cores sharing the last-level cache (= CCX) | L3 | `cache/index3/shared_cpu_list` | 4 |
| **package** | LLC domains sharing the on-package fabric | IO die / IF | `topology/physical_package_id` | 1 |
| **NUMA node** | packages/dies sharing a memory controller locally | interconnect + DRAM | `/sys/devices/system/node` | 1 |

Then a *pair* (or pool) is described by its **lowest common level** — the least-common-ancestor in that tree. Which turns the Setup line into something self-explanatory:

```
bench pin  [0, 12]  (2 slots, 2 hw threads on 1 core — shared L1/L2)
bench pin  [0, 1]   (2 slots, 2 hw threads on 2 cores, 1 LLC domain — shared L3)
bench pin  [0, 6]   (2 slots, 2 hw threads on 2 cores, 2 LLC domains — shared fabric only)
```

For bigger pools the same partition-count form scales: `--pin 0-5` → "6 hw threads on 6 cores, 2 LLC domains". And it composes with the `--pin smt` config-profile feature that already exists — profiles could be auto-generated from the discovered topology (`smt`, `llc`, `xllc`) instead of hand-listing CPU ids per machine, which would make the same experiment command portable between the 3900X and 7600X.

Terminology note for the docs when this lands: "CPU" is the word to *retire* from the report, precisely because your question was ambiguous in it — sysfs means hwt, colloquially it means core or even package. "Hardware thread", "core", "LLC domain" never collide. (Your experiment also showed why CCD earns no row: it's real silicon but adds no latency tier — the fabric is the fabric.)

Happy to write this up as the Todo entry — it's now three related pieces: topology discovery, the enriched bench-pin line, and topology-derived pin profiles.

The plain version: instead of "unique CPUs", describe any pinning by the deepest thing the threads share — same core (share L1/L2), same LLC domain (share L3), or same package (share only the interconnect) — since that's exactly what sets the speed. The names come straight from what Linux already exposes, "CPU" gets retired as ambiguous, and profiles like `--pin llc` could then work unchanged on any machine.

content.text:
"Logical CPU" / lCPU is a good pick — it's the kernel's own phrase (`Documentation/` and `lscpu` both use it), so the report vocabulary matches what users see in every other Linux tool. Here's the standardized table, with the vendor names demoted to examples — the key move that makes it portable is that **each level is defined by the resource shared, never by a vendor's marketing structure**:

| Term | Defined as | Shared resource | AMD x86 | Intel x86 | ARM | RISC-V |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **lCPU** | kernel-schedulable execution context | (is the unit) | SMT thread | hyperthread | typically 1:1 with core; SMT on some Neoverse | 1:1; SMT rare |
| **core** | lCPUs sharing L1 + execution engine | L1 (+private L2) | Zen core | P-core / E-core | Cortex/Neoverse core | hart group's core (U74 etc.) |
| **cluster** | cores sharing a mid-level cache | L2 (or L3 slice) | — (absent) | E-core module (4 cores/L2) | DynamIQ/DSU cluster | SiFive core complex (shared L2) |
| **LLC domain** | cores sharing the last-level cache | L3 / SLC | CCX | usually whole package (ring/mesh L3) | DSU L3 or system-level cache | shared L2/L3 cluster |
| **package** | LLC domains sharing on-package fabric | IO die / mesh / interconnect | Zen package | package | SoC | SoC/chiplet |
| **NUMA node** | packages with local memory | memory controller | NPS domains | sub-NUMA cluster | multi-socket/chiplet | multi-socket |

Four rules that keep it honest across all these designs:

1. **Levels collapse when absent.** AMD has no cluster level; on most Intel client parts LLC domain *equals* package (one shared L3) so the cross-LLC tier doesn't exist on-package; on SMT-less ARM, lCPU == core. The report should print only levels that actually partition the machine — discovery-driven, not a fixed six-row schema.
2. **The tree can be asymmetric.** On Alder-Lake-style hybrids, E-cores have a cluster level and P-cores don't; big.LITTLE mixes core types within one LLC domain. So it's a per-lCPU ancestry, not a uniform hierarchy — and core *type* (ARM's `cpu_capacity`, Intel's core kind) is an attribute on the core, orthogonal to the sharing tree.
3. **Discovery stays generic**: walk `cache/index*/shared_cpu_list` per lCPU and build domains from distinct sharing sets at each cache level, with `topology/{thread_siblings,cluster_cpus,package}_list` and `/sys/devices/system/node` filling the non-cache levels. That algorithm needs zero arch-specific code — cacheinfo is populated on ARM and increasingly on RISC-V; where it's missing, fall back to the topology files and mark cache levels unknown.
4. **Pairs are still described by nearest shared level** — that concept is untouched, just re-labelled: `[0,12] → 2 lCPUs, 1 core (shared L1/L2)`; `[0,6] → 2 lCPUs, 2 LLC domains (shared fabric)`.

This also incidentally matches the kernel's sched-domain ladder (SMT → CLS → MC → PKG → NUMA) one-to-one, which is decent evidence the level cut-points are the right ones — Linux has been forced to model every one of these machines already.

One naming nit to settle in the docs: with "lCPU" as the unit, `--pin` takes lCPU ids (as it already does), and the word "CPU" alone appears nowhere in output — each use becomes lCPU, core, or package as appropriate.

Want me to bank this as the Todo entry (topology discovery + terminology + enriched Setup line + auto-profiles, with this table as the design core)? It's grown into a well-shaped work item.

The plain version: adopt "lCPU" for the schedulable unit and describe machines as a nesting of lCPU → core → cluster → LLC domain → package → NUMA node, where each level is defined by what's shared (L1/L2, L2, L3, fabric, memory) rather than any vendor's names — vendor structures like CCX or E-core modules become examples of levels, levels that a given chip lacks simply don't appear, and the whole tree is discoverable at runtime from sysfs on every architecture we care about.

1	# Notes file conventions
2	
3	Conventions the bot follows when reading and writing notes files (`TODO.md`,
4	`notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`, `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One
5	source of truth lives here; [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
6	before editing a notes file.
7	
8	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
9	[custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## File reads: read the slice you need
12	
13	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs; grep or read
14	further on demand.
15	
16	- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
17	  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
18	  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`; read further only when chasing a
19	  lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
20	- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below the ranked
21	  `## Todo`). Read only when picking up a backlog item; grep to locate it first.
22	- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small; read whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
23	  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
24	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
25	  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
26	  need.
27	
28	**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
29	bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline; the same "slice you need" rule applies
30	to historical files.
31	
32	## Notes references
33	
34	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
35	for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
36	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
37	single-bracketed.
38	
39	## Reference numbering
40	
41	Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
42	file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
43	`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
44	completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.
45	
46	Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
47	`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
48	file's number; to cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
49	define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
50	span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
51	(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation; it needs no definition here. To
52	point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
53	`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.
54	
55	A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
56	`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
57	`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
58	as-built ladder. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
59	exact shape.
60	
61	A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
62	first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md`: `## Todo`
63	then `## Done`; `chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
64	appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
65	definitions move; every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
66	span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
67	namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule: `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
68	land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate; `chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are
69	append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
70	slots out of document order).
71	
72	## Markdown anchor links
73	
74	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
75	spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
76	(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
77	markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
78	official spec for auto-generated anchors; the de-facto reference implementation is
79	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
80	
81	## Todo format
82	
83	`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest;
84	long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
85	(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
86	description with reference links to more detail.
87	
88	`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
89	`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs` it's just
90	an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
91	reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
92	normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
93	durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
94	renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.
95	
96	Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
97	an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
98	fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
99	wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
100	title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.
101	
102	`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews; `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
103	`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.
104	
105	Example shape:
106	
107	```
108	# Todo
109	1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
110	2. Fix bug Y [[1]]
111	
112	# Done
113	- Fixed issue Z [[2]],[[3]]
114	
115	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
116	[2]: issues.md#issue-z
117	[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
118	```
119	
120	## Retiring Done entries
121	
122	`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
123	log. Move entries into `done.md` at two natural beats:
124	
125	- **Closing a ladder**: when the final `X.Y.Z` (no suffix) commit ships, decide which prior
126	  entries are no longer needed for nearby context and migrate them.
127	- **Opening a new ladder**: at `X.Y.Z-0`, do the same sweep before bumping the
128	  version-of-record.
129	
130	Migration mechanics:
131	
132	- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
133	  number).
134	- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
135	  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
136	- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
137	  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.
138	
139	## Chores conventions
140	
141	### Headings and entries that record a commit
142	
143	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records; see
144	[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
145	rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
146	`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. Titles carry **no
147	`(<version>)` suffix**; see
148	[Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description) for why. E.g. the chores
149	header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
150	`- refactor: extract config loader [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out commit's
151	title.
152	
153	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
154	`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section; those are named for
155	whatever fits. Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong default (nothing
156	absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.
157	
158	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress; the *last* edit before
159	`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
160	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm; the
161	pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
162	too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
163	
164	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
165	free-form text; the convention applies going forward.
166	
167	### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record
168	
169	A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header; see below), then
170	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
171	design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
172	per-file edit list. That lives in the commit message body, which is the source of truth for
173	"what changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally scoped to the commit). The
174	chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
175	restates the other.
176	
177	The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own rung to the as-built
178	ladder + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only
179	*finalizes*: header title sync, design subsections). Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in
180	cycle-protocol.md [Chores sections](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections); this note is
181	the pointer, so the two don't drift.
182	
183	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it;
184	promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
185	live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
186	`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
187	direction).
188	
189	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
190	places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
191	narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.
192	
193	### Chores commit references
194	
195	The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
196	commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
197	The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit; a single-commit cycle is a
198	one-rung ladder whose rung is the bare `X.Y.Z` close-out:
199	
200	```
201	## refactor: extract config loader
202	
203	- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser
204	- [[N]] 0.42.0 refactor: extract config loader
205	
206	<intro paragraph...>
207	```
208	
209	- The rung form is `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, with no `(current)` / `(done)` markers:
210	  as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
211	- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
212	  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
213	- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
214	  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
215	  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
216	  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
217	  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
218	  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
219	
220	```
221	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
222	```
223	
224	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
225	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
226	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
227	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
228	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
229	
230	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
231	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
232	can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung opens with the literal
233	`[[N]]` placeholder, and each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made
234	permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is the
235	record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
236	[Commits backfill](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
237	
238	Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines; the ladder form applies
239	going forward.
240	
241	### Chores file Table of Contents
242	
243	Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
244	first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
245	section, in file order.
246	
247	- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
248	  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
249	- Append the entry when the section opens; the entry text participates in the same last-edit
250	  title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
251	- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
252	- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.
253
