# Versioning

How this project versions its commits and the running
artifact. The scheme — the cycle step-numbering and the
unique-per-commit aim — is generic and shared across projects:
this file is copied **verbatim**, with
[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
covering each medium by conditional rather than per-project
edits.

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version** — the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`),
  written with `-` in prose, ladders, chores, todo, and commit
  talk; its suffix encodes the cycle phase (see
  [Step numbering](#step-numbering)).
- **version-of-record** — the authoritative stored copy of the
  version, in the project's manifest (see
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record));
  a built or running artifact derives from it.
- **versioning** — the topic: this scheme as a whole.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and
surfaced, and how often it changes — pick the case that fits
your medium:

- **Manifest** — where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the
    committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic
    `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter, …) — add the case as
    needed
- **Notation** — how the `-` form is stored:
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`),
    store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python
    project), remap to `+` — `0.3.0-5.3.0` → `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same
    version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter** — how a built artifact surfaces the
  version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence** — how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement);
  this project follows the per-commit preference.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change
on **every commit**, so a built or running artifact identifies
the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project
  following the cycle protocol may bump less often — once per
  cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
  if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are
  **pre-assignable**, unlike the git SHA, which a commit cannot
  contain (see the cycle protocol's
  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).

## Step numbering

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out; see
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes each commit's
phase in the version suffix — the **final identifier `0` marks
a Preparation**:

- `X.Y.Z-0` — Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, … — Work commits
- `X.Y.Z` — Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle — no ladder,
no setup commit — skips `-0` and starts at `-1` (its first
Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that
grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step without
renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10` — Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a
  Preparation.
- `-1.0` — Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final
  identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0` — Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2` — its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3` — its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0` — Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of each phase, so the
active phase is recorded — and, per the preference above,
every commit carries a distinct version.

35

40	   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.

42	   complete.
43	6. Write the description: <=72-col conventional title, prose body (work repo: file-by-file,
44	   opening with the version-bump bullet). See
45	   [Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
46	7. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
47	   explicitly includes it.
48	8. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
49	   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

[custom.md](../custom.md).

(`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...) -> Close-out (bare `X.Y.Z`). The version suffix encodes the phase;
the scheme, and where the version-of-record lives, are in
[versioning.md](../notes/versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](../notes/cycle-protocol.md)
before any commit work, and before any push, cycle or not.

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`; never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)); a
pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate (bugs.md #6). In
an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.

4. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
5. Say "ready to commit" and stop. The user reviews the working-copy diff; iterate until
   complete.
6. Write the description: <=72-col conventional title, prose body (work repo: file-by-file,
   opening with the version-bump bullet). See
   [Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
7. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
8. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist

Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
[per-Work-commit contract](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
   the one permitted describe; the commit is never published and never carries a trailer.

Nothing on a ladder is pushed; the close-out squash
(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
publishes the single commit.

## Before any push

- Closing words are already written; nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).

## After the final push: hard stop

Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing

after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
push. See
[After push or squash-push](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

## Close-out checklist

[Close-out](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#close-out):

1. Move the picked-up item from `## In Progress` to a one-line `## Done` entry with its chores

2. Finalize the chores section: sync the header to the final commit title (and every anchor

   [in the protocol](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe); its step 4 is

- [[N]] 0.24.1 docs: explain the grade columns and the blocks/batches nesting

The 0.24.1 single-commit cycle: make the report decodable
without assembling the answer from 160 lines of prose. Grown
from a 2026-08-01 session reading `zcr-with-2t` pinning
experiments, where the grade block and the blocks/batches
relationship both needed explaining in conversation.

- **column reference in README**: a compact per-column list
  directly under the grade-block example in "The two grades",
  one bullet per column stating which rows it applies to and
  what it measures; the existing sections keep the depth
- **blocks nest above batches**, stated at both places a
  reader looks: the README `--blocks` bullet and the `--blocks`
  help text. Batches are the grade block's contiguous
  time-series grain; blocks are the CI's sleep-separated
  replication grain; each block is a contiguous stretch of
  whole batches
- **a blank line before the grade block** separates it from
  the summary rows, on every report
- rides along: the "Topology-aware pinning and lCPU
  terminology" Todo entry (the session's pinning-experiment
  findings: SMT ~35 ns, same-CCX ~133 ns, cross-CCX ~633 ns on
  the 3900X), and the punctuation-sweep pickup moved to
  `## In Progress` as the next cycle

vc-x1 0.71.0

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main` — one resumable command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (tracking / bot-published / sync checks —
no build steps; run project checks yourself before pushing)
→ review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-work → commit-bot (skipped if clean) → bookmark-set
(work repo → <bookmark>, bot repo → main) → push-work →
squash-push-bot. Failures in commit-work / commit-bot /
bookmark-set roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-work.
After push-work succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (flag form; see positional)

  -V, --version
          Print the `vc-x1 X.Y.Z` banner as the first line, then continue. With
          no subcommand, prints the banner and exits.
          
          Replaces clap's auto-version (which would exit after printing): the
          banner now rides along with normal subcommand execution rather than
          gating it, so scripts can capture the version *and* the command's
          output in one invocation.

      --restart
          Clear any saved state file and start from stage 1

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --from <STAGE>
          Explicit stage to jump to (advanced / debug use)

          Possible values:
          - preflight:       Verify bookmark tracking, the bot-published
            invariant, and sync state
          - review:          Present diff for the first approval gate
          - message:         Compose / edit the commit message; present for
            second gate
          - commit-work:     Commit the work repo
          - commit-bot:      Commit the `.claude` bot repo (skipped if empty)
          - bookmark-set:    Advance each repo's bookmark to its `@-`: work →
            `<bookmark>`, bot → `main`
          - push-work:       `jj git push --bookmark <b> -R .`
          - squash-push-bot: In-process squash of `.claude`'s trailing session
            writes + push `main`

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate

      --status
          Print where the saved state thinks we are and exit

      --recheck
          Re-run `preflight` even on resume (default: skip if last run
          succeeded)

      --no-squash-push
          Stop before `squash-push-bot` so it can be run manually

      --dry-run
          Print the exact commands for every stage without side effects

      --title <STR>
          Commit title (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

      --body <STR>
          Commit body (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

  -y, --yes
          Auto-approve interactive prompts (review gate, message-edit
          confirmation). Required when `--title` / `--body` aren't both supplied
          in non-interactive contexts

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

content.content:
1	# jj and cross-repo linking
2	
3	How version control is driven on this project (jj, never raw git) and how the two repos'
4	commits point at each other (the `ochid:` trailer). Read this before any jj operation beyond
5	`st` / `log` / `diff`, and always before touching a commit description.
6	
7	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
8	[custom.md](../custom.md).
9	
10	## jj Basics
11	
12	**Use jj, not git, for version-control operations** (status, log, diff, commit, push, history
13	rewrite). jj coexists with the git backend, so the repo *can* be driven with raw `git`, but
14	this project's workflow (bookmarks, the working-copy `@` model, ochid trailers) is expressed in
15	jj terms; reaching for `git` invites state that doesn't match the jj documentation here. There
16	is no `jj mv`: to move/rename a tracked file, just `mv` it on disk and jj detects the rename by
17	content.
18	
19	- `jj st -R .` / `jj st -R .claude`: show working copy status
20	- `jj log -R .` / `jj log -R .claude`: show commit log
21	- `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: finalize working copy into a commit
22	- `jj describe -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: set description without committing
23	- `jj git push --bookmark <name> -R <repo>`: push a bookmark (no `--allow-new` flag; jj pushes
24	  new bookmarks without special flags)
25	- In jj, the working copy (@) is always a mutable commit being edited. `jj commit` finalizes it
26	  and creates a new empty working copy on top.
27	- The bot repo always has uncommitted changes during an active session because session data
28	  updates continuously.
29	- `jj rebase` uses `--onto`/`-o` to name the destination(s).
30	
31	## Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)
32	
33	The cross-reference between the work repo and the bot repo is what makes the dual-repo work:
34	every commit points at its counterpart in the other repo, so the "what" (code) and the
35	"why / how" (session) stay linked across time. That pointer is the **ochid** (Other Change ID)
36	git trailer.
37	
38	A **chid** is jj's change ID, a permanent identifier that survives rebases and `describe`s
39	(unlike the commit ID / git SHA, which changes on rewrite). An **ochid** trailer carries the
40	counterpart commit's chid as a workspace-root-relative path:
41	
42	- Paths start with `/`, the workspace root, i.e. the work repo (the project root). `/.claude`
43	  is the bot sub-repo.
44	- `ochid: /<chid>` references a change in the **work repo**.
45	- `ochid: /.claude/<chid>` references a change in the **bot repo**.
46	
47	Trailers are blank-line-separated `key: value` lines at the end of the commit body, using the
48	chid's **12-character** prefix:
49	
50	```
51	ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqowktp   # points to a bot-repo change
52	ochid: /wtpmottvxqzl           # points to a work-repo change
53	```
54	
55	How many, and which direction:
56	
57	- **Work-repo commits** each carry one `ochid: /.claude/<bot-chid>`, the bot repo's change ID.
58	- **The bot-repo commit** carries one `ochid: /<work-chid>` per work-repo commit in that push.
59	  The count is per *push*, not per cycle. A trapezoid close-out whose rungs were pushed 1:1 as
60	  they landed still carries exactly one; more than one occurs when a single push publishes
61	  several work-repo commits.
62	
63	Use `vc-x1 chid -s work,bot -L` to capture the change IDs (first line work repo, second bot
64	repo).
65	
66	`ochid:` trailers are **stamped by `vc-x1 push`**; never hand-write them into a commit body or
67	`--title`/`--body`.
68

# jj and cross-repo linking

How version control is driven on this project (jj, never raw git) and how the two repos'
commits point at each other (the `ochid:` trailer). Read this before any jj operation beyond
`st` / `log` / `diff`, and always before touching a commit description.

Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## jj Basics

**Use jj, not git, for version-control operations** (status, log, diff, commit, push, history
rewrite). jj coexists with the git backend, so the repo *can* be driven with raw `git`, but
this project's workflow (bookmarks, the working-copy `@` model, ochid trailers) is expressed in
jj terms; reaching for `git` invites state that doesn't match the jj documentation here. There
is no `jj mv`: to move/rename a tracked file, just `mv` it on disk and jj detects the rename by
content.

- `jj st -R .` / `jj st -R .claude`: show working copy status
- `jj log -R .` / `jj log -R .claude`: show commit log
- `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: finalize working copy into a commit
- `jj describe -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>`: set description without committing
- `jj git push --bookmark <name> -R <repo>`: push a bookmark (no `--allow-new` flag; jj pushes
  new bookmarks without special flags)
- In jj, the working copy (@) is always a mutable commit being edited. `jj commit` finalizes it
  and creates a new empty working copy on top.
- The bot repo always has uncommitted changes during an active session because session data
  updates continuously.
- `jj rebase` uses `--onto`/`-o` to name the destination(s).

## Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)

The cross-reference between the work repo and the bot repo is what makes the dual-repo work:
every commit points at its counterpart in the other repo, so the "what" (code) and the
"why / how" (session) stay linked across time. That pointer is the **ochid** (Other Change ID)
git trailer.

A **chid** is jj's change ID, a permanent identifier that survives rebases and `describe`s
(unlike the commit ID / git SHA, which changes on rewrite). An **ochid** trailer carries the
counterpart commit's chid as a workspace-root-relative path:

- Paths start with `/`, the workspace root, i.e. the work repo (the project root). `/.claude`
  is the bot sub-repo.
- `ochid: /<chid>` references a change in the **work repo**.
- `ochid: /.claude/<chid>` references a change in the **bot repo**.

Trailers are blank-line-separated `key: value` lines at the end of the commit body, using the
chid's **12-character** prefix:

```
ochid: /.claude/xvzvruqowktp   # points to a bot-repo change
ochid: /wtpmottvxqzl           # points to a work-repo change
```

How many, and which direction:

- **Work-repo commits** each carry one `ochid: /.claude/<bot-chid>`, the bot repo's change ID.
- **The bot-repo commit** carries one `ochid: /<work-chid>` per work-repo commit in that push.
  The count is per *push*, not per cycle. A trapezoid close-out whose rungs were pushed 1:1 as
  they landed still carries exactly one; more than one occurs when a single push publishes
  several work-repo commits.

Use `vc-x1 chid -s work,bot -L` to capture the change IDs (first line work repo, second bot
repo).

`ochid:` trailers are **stamped by `vc-x1 push`**; never hand-write them into a commit body or
`--title`/`--body`.

## Re-describing: coordinate first, and keep the trailer

**Never `jj describe` a commit that is already published or already carries trailers without
coordinating with everyone involved first.** It is a history rewrite, and it silently drops the
cross-repo link. Describing a fresh local commit that has never been described and carries no
trailers is authoring a message rather than rewriting one, and is not covered; that is the
sub-cycle ladder's
[per-Work-commit contract](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder)
step 4.

When a re-describe is agreed, copy any `ochid:` trailers into the new body by hand (the "don't
hand-write trailers" rule covers push authoring a message from scratch, not preserving one
already stamped). Hit at the 0.77.2 amend (2026-07-29), where the trailer survived only that
way; `vc-x1 fix-desc` repairs a dropped one by title match.

## Resolvability

A change ID travels with its commit: a **pushed** commit resolves to the same chid in every
clone; cloning the bot repo gave the published `main` tip the same chid as an existing clone.
We think jj carries the change ID in the git commit object, so it survives `jj git clone` /
fetch.

The local-only case is the **working-copy `@`**: jj mints a fresh random chid for `@` in each
clone, so an unpushed `@` is never a stable ochid target. This is why a bot-repo ochid names
`@-` (the last committed change), not `@`.

## .vc-config.toml

Each repo contains a `.vc-config.toml` whose `[repos]` registry records the workspace layout.
Values are ordinary paths relative to the config file's directory (absolute allowed,
discouraged), so the two sides' blocks **differ**: the entry that resolves to the config's own
directory names its side, and the two sides must agree on the same resolved work/bot pair:

```toml
# work side          # bot side
[repos]              [repos]
work = "."           work = ".."
bot = ".claude"      bot = "."
```

Ochid trailer prefixes are fixed per-side labels (`/` work, `/.claude` bot) resolved by side
detection, not filesystem paths.

1	# iiac-perf
2	
3	A general-purpose latency microbenchmark harness for Rust. Each
4	bench runs against a wall-clock time budget with auto-sized loop
5	counts and reports a percentile-band histogram in nanoseconds.
6	
7	Numbers are raw: nothing is subtracted, so a column is what the
8	apparatus measured. The apparatus does cost something (a timer
9	pair plus the loop that drives it), and the inner loop is sized
10	so that cost is a small fraction of the workload's, which is what
11	makes a raw number usable rather than merely honest. What the
12	harness will not do is estimate that cost and subtract it: the
13	estimate is ill-defined at this scale, and it cancels anyway in
14	the same-harness A/B comparison the tool exists for.
15	
16	Highlights:
17	
18	- Time-based runs (`-d SECONDS` per bench, `-D SECONDS` total)
19	  with auto-sized outer/inner loop counts.
20	- Band-based histogram (min→p1, p1→p10, …, p99→max) with count,
21	  mean, and range.
22	- Per-run grades for the workload and for the machine, each
23	  computed from the run's own data.
24	- Per-thread CPU pinning (`--pin`), independent of the pin used
25	  for the startup tick-rate warm (`--no-pin-cal`).
26	- Plug in new workloads by implementing the `Bench` trait and
27	  registering in `src/benches/`.
28	
29	The first benches measure Inter-Intra Application Communication
30	(function calls, async calls, channels, serde), which is what
31	seeded the project name. The harness itself is workload-agnostic.
32	The `ice-*` benches measure iceoryx2 shared-memory IPC inside one
33	process, in both of its messaging patterns (`ice-ps-*`
34	publish/subscribe, `ice-rr-*` request/response) at one and two
35	threads.
36	
37	## Design (0.2.0)
38	
39	Design a Rust app that can measure the cost of various (IIAC) techniques.
40	By IIAC I mean all communication techniques between and within
41	applications such as regular function calls vs async function calls vs
42	channels vs serde/deser of json or zero-copy messaging using io_uring and
43	potentially any other technique. It would include between threads or
44	processes or apps on the same computer or between apps on the same LAN or
45	between apps over a WAN.
46	
47	Ideally I'd like to be able to see a histogram of the range of times of the
48	send and receive costs, not just the mean/average of 10^3 or 10^6 invocations.
49	So the cost of the work should or could be something near-zero such as just
50	echoing the input, but maybe there is value in doing some constant but
51	variable amount of work to verify it's in-consequential. One thing I think we
52	need to be aware of is that if we make the work too simple the compiler could
53	just keep things in registers which would not be representative of "real" work.
54	
55	We should start simple, like comparing normal and async function calls and
56	later expand to other techniques.
57	
58	## Usage
59	
60	```
61	iiac-perf [BENCH...] [-d SECONDS] [-o OUTER] [-i INNER]
62	iiac-perf qualify-environment [--runs N] [--gap SECONDS] [-d SECONDS]
63	iiac-perf add-completion-yaml
64	```
65	
66	`BENCH` is one or more registered bench names, or `all` for every
67	registered bench. A name that matches no bench exactly runs every
68	bench it is a prefix of: `ice` runs all iceoryx2 benches, `mpsc`
69	runs `mpsc-1t` and `mpsc-2t`. **With no arguments, `iiac-perf` prints the
70	available list and exits, and that's the source of truth for which
71	benches the current build registers.**
72	
73	`iiac-perf qualify-environment` (also stand-alone) asks whether
74	this **machine** is fit to measure on:
75	it respawns this binary `--runs` times (default 10) at `--gap`
76	seconds apart, collects each run's environment grade, prints the
77	table, and gives a verdict, exiting nonzero when the machine
78	does not qualify. Use it to characterize a box before trusting
79	numbers from it.
80	
81	What it runs is, in metrology terms, a repeatability study of the
82	apparatus plus the machine, which is why the grading module is
83	called `gauge`.
84	
85	```
86	  run   warmup  bench    worst   settle   mean
87	  1     A       A        A       0.86s    22.2 ns
88	  2     D       A        D       1.31s    22.2 ns
89	  3     A       C        C       0.61s    22.5 ns
90	
91	  median environment grade: A
92	  median settle: 0.86s (0 of 3 never settled)
93	  transition-degraded (drift or step at D/F): 1 of 3
94	
95	  verdict: NOT QUALIFIED
96	    a state transition landed inside a measurement window
97	```
98	
99	It reads the environment grade rather than the run grade,
100	because the subject is the box: `warmup` is its settling
101	behaviour across respawns, `bench` whether it then held. The
102	verdict is grades, not values: median at B or better, and no
103	run whose `drift` or `step` reached D/F, those two being the
104	transition detectors. `spread` and `interference` wobble is
105	ambient contamination and does not fail a run. The `mean` column
106	is informational, and it is where a two-state machine shows
107	itself at a glance.
108	
109	The `settle` column is how long each child's warmup took to
110	reach the state it measured in (`not` when it never did — see
111	[Settle time](#settle-time)). It is reported, not judged: a box
112	still moving when warmup ended already shows up as a `drift` or
113	`step` D/F on the warmup stretch, so a second criterion would
114	only restate the first. What it adds is the size of the number —
115	how much `--settle-time` this box actually wants.
116	
117	Each child runs `min-now` for `-d` seconds (default 1): the box
118	is the subject, so the leanest bench is the right one. `--pin`
119	and `--settle-time` pass through to the children, and
120	`--print-only` prints the table without deciding a verdict.
121	
122	`iiac-perf add-completion-yaml` (also stand-alone) installs the
123	carapace completion spec: Tab then completes bench names, command
124	words, and flags in any carapace-served shell. Without it,
125	`iiac-perf ice<TAB>` has nothing to offer and bench names must
126	be typed (or copied from the no-args listing) by hand. Run it
127	once after installing iiac-perf, and again after an upgrade
128	that changes flags or command words; new benches never need a
129	re-run. See [Shell completion](#shell-completion).
130	
131	Flags (also visible via `-h` / `--help`):
132	- `-d`, `--duration SECONDS`: target wall-clock seconds per bench
133	  (default `5.0`); the outer loop runs until this time is reached
134	  (inner auto-sizes). See chores `0.3.1-dev1` for the empirical
135	  study behind the default; longer (`-d 30`+) gives
136	  publication-grade stability. Mutually exclusive with `-D`.
137	- `-D`, `--total-duration SECONDS`: target total wall-clock seconds
138	  across all requested benches; budget is split equally per bench
139	  (e.g. `-D 30` with 6 benches -> 5 s each). Mutually exclusive with
140	  `-d`.
141	- `-o`, `--outer N`: override outer loop count (forces count-based
142	  mode instead of time-based; inner still adapts).
143	- `-i`, `--inner N`: override inner loop count per histogram sample.
144	  `inner=1` measures single-call latency (each sample = one step).
145	  Higher inner measures back-to-back / burst rate (each sample = N
146	  steps averaged, hides per-call jitter and parking costs).
147	- `--pin CORES`: pin bench threads to logical CPUs. `CORES` is a
148	  comma-separated list with optional ranges: `0,1`, `0-5`, `0,3-5,7`.
149	  Treated as a **core pool** indexed positionally with wrap-around, so
150	  thread `i` gets `pool[i % pool.len()]`. Examples:
151	  - `--pin 0,1` pins a 2-thread bench to logical CPUs 0 and 1.
152	  - `--pin 0,0` co-locates two threads on the same CPU
153	    (oversubscription, which measures contention).
154	  - `--pin 0-11` defines a 12-CPU pool for larger fanout benches;
155	    threads wrap over it.
156	
157	  A `CORES` value that names a `[profiles]` entry in the
158	  [config file](#config-file) expands to that profile's core spec,
159	  `--pin smt` with `smt = "0,12"` configured is exactly `--pin 0,12`.
160	  A value that isn't a profile name is parsed directly as cores, so
161	  raw specs keep working.
162

# custom.md - iiac-perf's project layer

## Medium and validation

`iiac-perf`); versioning specifics in [versioning.md](notes/versioning.md).

  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
    1. `cargo fmt`
    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
    3. `cargo test`
    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
- **Fast validation**
  - when: ladder checklist step 3
  - `cargo test --bins`
- **Pipelines hide failures**
  - never pipe a validating command into `tail`/`grep`
  - never `&&` after a piped stage: a pipeline's status is the last command's
  - `${PIPESTATUS[0]}`: the escape hatch when a pipe is genuinely wanted

## Project conventions and overrides

- **Installed vc-x1 predates the `code` -> `work` scope rename** (checked 2026-07-31)
  - overrides the scope note in [AGENTS.md Terminology](AGENTS.md#the-dual-repo-model): use
    `--scope=code|bot|code,bot` with the installed binary
  - retire this entry when vc-x1 is upgraded past the rename
- **Acquaint routine addition: check the mailbox** (adopted 2026-07-31)
  - on acquaint, check `../vc-x1-template/messages/iiac-perf.md`; an absent file means no mail
  - the message protocol is `../vc-x1-template/MESSAGES.md`

  - the pre-restructure AGENTS.md permitted `jj commit` plus a hand-written `ochid:` for a
    commit pushed later as a non-top commit, on the ground that push stamps only the topmost

    behavior on multi-commit pushes is verified; if push stamps every commit it creates, the

content.text:
Thoughts, no action taken:

**The mechanics are expensive: this isn't a renumber, it's a rewrite of published history.** 0.24.0 and 0.24.1 are pushed to origin/main, and the version-of-record lives *inside* them (`Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock` content). Changing their versions means rewriting file content of two published commits — new SHAs for both plus every descendant, a force-push, and hard rule 4 territory (rewriting published, trailer-carrying commits) where the ochid trailers survive only by hand-copying. The knock-on set is real: chores-05's just-backfilled refs [[12]] and [[13]] record the current SHAs and would both be invalidated; the bot-repo commits' ochids still resolve (chids survive rewrites) but the recorded 40-hex SHAs don't. The 0.23.0 trapezoid experiment proved this *can* be done — but that reshape changed no file contents, and its one casualty was exactly a recorded SHA. This would be two content rewrites, so two invalidated refs, plus every textual mention of "0.24.0"/"0.24.1" across chores-05, TODO Done entries, custom.md's dogfood log, and README's example banners — and the session transcripts in the bot repo that quote `iiac-perf 0.24.0` reports can't be rewritten at all, so record and history would permanently disagree.

**On the merits, I'd also argue 0.24.0 earned its minor.** The convention as recorded says functional work bumps the minor, docs bumps the patch. The grade-block compaction was a `feat:` that restructured src/ — renderer *and* the `qualify.rs` parser that consumes the format. Report structure is an interface here (the selftest parses it positionally), and interface changes are functional in the sense that matters. 0.24.1 sits closer to the line (it did touch src/, cosmetically), but patch was defensible as "nothing measured or computed changed."

**What I think the itch actually is**: the convention's word "functional" is under-defined, and these three cycles exposed it. The cheap, honest fix is forward-looking: sharpen the custom.md entry rather than rewrite history. Something like — *patch: no change to what is measured, how numbers are computed, or any parsed output format (docs, notes, cosmetic framing); minor: changes to measurement, statistics, CLI surface, or report structure.* Under that test, 0.24.0 minor / 0.24.1 patch / 0.24.2 patch — the numbers as they stand — come out consistent.

**If you do want the renumber anyway**, the honest scope is: coordinate first (rule 4), rewrite both commits' Cargo.toml/lock + descriptions with trailers hand-preserved, re-backfill [[12]]/[[13]], sweep every "0.24.x" mention in the notes, force-push, and accept that bot-repo transcripts keep the old numbers. It's an afternoon of careful work purchasing aesthetic continuity in a pre-1.0 version line — my recommendation is to spend that afternoon elsewhere.

The plain version: the two earlier versions are already published with the numbers baked into their contents, so changing them means rewriting shared history and fixing every place the old numbers were written down — and some places (session logs) can't be fixed at all. I'd keep 0.24.x, land this as 0.24.2, and instead tighten the written rule about what deserves a minor versus a patch so future numbering never feels off.

content.text:
With that constraint removed, my assessment genuinely changes — most of my objection last turn was the published-history cost, and a single-user repo with no external clones makes that a bounded internal cleanup rather than a coordination hazard. Remaining thoughts:

**It becomes feasible and modest in scope.** The honest task list: rewrite the two pushed commits' `Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock` (and their described versions where mentioned), hand-preserving the ochid trailers (rule 4's procedure — and you *are* the coordination it requires); force-push main; re-backfill chores refs [[12]]/[[13]] with the new SHAs; sweep the ~15-20 textual "0.24.0"/"0.24.1" mentions across chores-05, the TODO Done entries, and my pending 0.24.2 section; renumber the pending close-out to 0.23.4 before it pushes. A useful property working in our favor: jj chids survive rewrites, so the bot-repo side's ochid links stay valid untouched — only the work-repo side needs care. One thing stays unfixable: this session's transcripts and pasted reports carry `iiac-perf 0.24.0/0.24.1` banners forever. I'd record the old→new mapping in the dogfood log so a future reader of those transcripts isn't confused.

**Decide the rule before renumbering, or the numbers will drift again.** The renumber is only worth doing if it's the *consequence of a written rule*, not a one-off aesthetic fix. The rule that makes 0.23.2/3/4 coherent is: **minor = changes to what is measured or how numbers are computed; everything else — docs, presentation, report layout, parsers of our own output — is patch.** That's a perfectly defensible alternative to my "format is an interface" reading, and it's your call to make. Written into custom.md alongside the renumber, the three cycles come out consistent and future cycles have a test to apply.

**The branch-first process is the better half of this message, and the protocol already anticipates it.** cycle-protocol.md's backfill rule explicitly says topic-branch sections wait to record SHAs until the branch lands — the "permanent branch" concept is already load-bearing. Formalizing "cycles happen on a topic bookmark, `main` only advances by landing" buys exactly the freedom you're exercising now, routinely and without ceremony: everything on the bookmark stays rewritable until landed, version numbers can be corrected pre-merge, and force-pushes to main stop existing as a concept. `vc-x1 push` takes an arbitrary bookmark already, so the tooling gap is small — mainly a "land" step (ff main to the bookmark) and the discipline of not pushing main directly. That's a custom.md process entry plus a template finding, and I'd make it a Todo either way, because it converts today's special case into the normal case.

**Sequencing note if you go ahead**: the renumber should happen *before* the pending 0.24.2 push — the working copy still references 0.24.1's SHA in a backfill and carries version 0.24.2, so doing history first means the close-out lands once, correctly, as 0.23.4, instead of being rewritten immediately after landing.

The plain version: with nobody else pulling from this repo, rewriting the two published versions is safe and takes maybe an hour including the record sweep — the only permanent leftover is that this session's saved output quotes the old numbers. But do it only together with writing down the rule that produces the new numbers, so the question never comes back; and adopt the work-on-a-branch habit regardless, since it makes exactly this kind of correction free in the future.

message.content: I guess the rule is since in rust semver are three fields and we are iterating fairly quickly our minor number is rising kinda fast and these are single step "tweaks" multi-step bumping minor feels natural but even that isn't a good reason. I think it's a minor should be on "scope" size. So adding a new bench or incremental functionality, patch change. Changing architecture minor bump. Thoughts

content.text:
Scope-based is, I think, the right family of rule for this project — and it's actually more honest than both my "measurement semantics" test and the original "functional vs docs" split. Thoughts:

**Why it fits**: iiac-perf's version isn't a compatibility contract (it's a binary, not a published library dep — nobody writes `iiac-perf = "0.24"`), so the number's real job is communication: "which era of the tool produced this report". Eras are architectural. Under your rule the minor number tracks *reshapings* — 0.22→0.23 was raw-batch grading replacing calibration, a genuine era boundary — while patch absorbs the steady stream of benches, tweaks, and docs. That also fixes the symptom you named: minor stops inflating just because iteration is fast, and a rising patch number is cheap (0.23.17 costs nothing).

**You're right to reject step-count as the proxy.** Single- vs multi-rung is landing mechanics, not scope — a big architectural change can land as one squashed commit, and a ladder can be ten incremental tweaks. The two axes are independent, and the grade-block cycle (multi-file, single-commit, purely presentational) is the proof case.

**The one weakness to shore up: "architecture" is fuzzier than "measurement changed", so give it a test.** Suggestion: *did the shape of the system change, or just its contents?* Minor = restructuring how the harness measures, grades, or is organized — a subsystem added or removed, the pipeline reshaped, the report contract redesigned. Patch = work within the existing shape — new benches, incremental flags, presentation, docs, notes. Running the backlog through it as a calibration check: raw-batch grading → minor (it was). Grade-block compaction → patch (your renumber, consistent). New bench like `ice-ps-2t-wait` → patch. Dynamic startup warmup (Todo #1) → minor (replaces the warmup architecture). Topology-aware pinning → minor (new discovery subsystem + report vocabulary). The seam-offload SPSC work → minor (pipeline reshape). Those all land where intuition says they should, which is the sign the test is cutting in the right place.

**Two footnotes**: first, if the crate ever splits out a library (the workspace idea in `## Ideas`), revisit — cargo treats 0.x minors as breaking boundaries for *dependents*, and the rule would need to grow a compat clause. Second, the rule retro-validates the proposed renumber exactly: 0.23.2 (grade block, presentation), 0.23.3 (report docs), 0.23.4 (punctuation) — all contents-not-shape, all patches, and 0.24.0 stays reserved for the next real reshaping.

So: adopt it, word it with the shape-vs-contents test, and it belongs in custom.md's conventions right next to (replacing) the minor-vs-patch entry I added this cycle — which would make the renumber the rule's first application rather than a one-off. Say the word and I'll fold the convention rewrite into the pending close-out, and we can plan the history rewrite as its own careful step before pushing.

# custom.md - iiac-perf's project layer

The one agent-editable instruction file (see [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#custommd-the-project-layer)).
Loaded after AGENTS.md; on conflict, this file wins.

## Medium and validation

The artifact is the `iiac-perf` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name
`iiac-perf`); versioning specifics in [versioning.md](notes/versioning.md).

- **Full validation**
  - when: per-commit checklist step 4; skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out
  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
    1. `cargo fmt`
    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
    3. `cargo test`
    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
- **Fast validation**
  - when: ladder checklist step 3
  - `cargo test --bins`
- **Pipelines hide failures**
  - never pipe a validating command into `tail`/`grep`
  - never `&&` after a piped stage: a pipeline's status is the last command's
  - `${PIPESTATUS[0]}`: the escape hatch when a pipe is genuinely wanted

## Project conventions and overrides

- **Version advancement: functional work bumps the minor,
  non-functional (docs/notes) bumps the patch** (decided 2026-07-29
  picking 0.23.1; recorded here 2026-08-01, rescued from the parked
  punctuation-sweep branch's "absorb versioning.md" Todo entry)
  - versioning.md specifies only the suffix scheme; this is the
    project's `X.Y.Z` advancement choice
  - `Z` had never left `0` before 0.23.1 only because every prior
    cycle was functional

- **Installed vc-x1 predates the `code` -> `work` scope rename** (checked 2026-07-31)
  - overrides the scope note in [AGENTS.md Terminology](AGENTS.md#the-dual-repo-model): use
    `--scope=code|bot|code,bot` with the installed binary
  - retire this entry when vc-x1 is upgraded past the rename
- **Acquaint routine addition: check the mailbox** (adopted 2026-07-31)
  - on acquaint, check `../vc-x1-template/messages/iiac-perf.md`; an absent file means no mail
  - the message protocol is `../vc-x1-template/MESSAGES.md`
- **Non-top-commit ochid exception dropped pending verification** (2026-07-31)
  - the pre-restructure AGENTS.md permitted `jj commit` plus a hand-written `ochid:` for a
    commit pushed later as a non-top commit, on the ground that push stamps only the topmost
    commit
  - hard rule 5 (never hand-write ochids) governs until `vc-x1 push`'s actual stamping
    behavior on multi-commit pushes is verified; if push stamps every commit it creates, the
    exception stays dead, otherwise raise it as a template finding

## Dogfood log

Dated entries on where these instructions chafed, failed, or got amended; the evidence base
for the promotion decision in the template repository (vc-x1-template).

- 2026-08-01: `vc-x1 push --body` rejects a body whose first character is `-`
  - a file-by-file body opening with its first bullet failed twice: once at vc-x1's own clap
    (worked around with `--body=`), then again inside push's `jj commit -m <body>` (same clap
    leading-hyphen rejection), which rolled both repos back cleanly
  - workaround that also satisfies prose form: open the body with its intro line, never a
    bare bullet
  - template finding: vc-x1 should pass bodies to jj as `-m=<body>` or via stdin/file

- 2026-07-31: adopted mid-dogfood-window
  - adoption base: the template's `AGENTS-vc-x1-f5-20260730-snapshot/` (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md,
    agent-data/), created the same day from vc-x1's live copy, the window's authority
  - local copies verified byte-identical to the snapshot at adoption (`diff -r`)
- 2026-07-31: adoption base amended before first commit
  - the snapshot's AGENTS.md gained rule 0 (read custom.md before acting) and hard-rules-first
    ordering; authored snapshot-side while vc-x1's session was live, with the pending sync to
    vc-x1 tracked in the template's snapshots.md
  - local AGENTS.md re-copied from the snapshot; pin set re-verified byte-identical
- 2026-07-31: template restructured into vc-x1-template; pin lines made generic
  - the template + coordination point is now the vc-x1-template repo: init payload in `work/`
    and `work.claude/`, discussion artifacts in `agents-protocol/`, mailboxes in `messages/`;
    the old vc-x1-work-repo-template and vc-x1-bot-repo-template are untouched pending wink's
    discussion with vc-x1
  - every "pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template" line in the pin set became "the template
    repository" (snapshot-side amendment, same pending-sync flow as rule 0)
  - local pin set re-copied; snapshot, `work/`, and this repo verified three-way byte-identical
- 2026-07-31: first push under the new rules; two checklist gaps found (the 0.23.1 push)
  - given "desc and push", the agent jumped straight to the description: cycle.md's per-commit
    checklist has no step for backfilling the previous push's chores refs, bumping the
    version-of-record, or appending the chores record, so following it verbatim skips all
    three. Proposed template fix: add them as explicit steps before "write the description"
  - rule adopted (wink): **every commit belongs to a cycle, single- or multi-commit; there is
    no out-of-cycle push.** Mid-ladder the cycle is implied; otherwise ask "single- or
    multi-step cycle?" before preparing the commit. A single-commit cycle is a bare `X.Y.Z`
    close-out, so its validation is mandatory, and with no planning phase it skips
    `## In Progress` and goes straight to chores + Done
  - convention adopted (wink): chores commit references use the **as-built ladder form** for
    every cycle (rung `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`), replacing the `Commits:` line; codified in
    agent-data/notes.md + cycle.md (snapshot-side, pending vc-x1 sync) and both
    cycle-protocol.md copies (this repo's and the template payload's); pre-existing
    `Commits:` lines are grandfathered
  - convention adopted (wink): chores files carry a **title-only `## Table of Contents`**, one
    `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording section; no versions or refs, so it
    never needs backfill (the TOC navigates, the ladder records); codified beside the ladder
    form, first instance in chores-05.md
- 2026-07-31: Todo #1 run as a single-commit cycle after a four-rung ladder was rejected
  - the proposed rungs split along implementation lines (print+parser / precision / README)
    and failed the test that makes a ladder worth having: no rung was independently valuable
    or revertable, and every intermediate state was a half-reshaped published report
  - refines the single-vs-multi question: multi-commit wants rungs that each stand alone;
    "one deliverable, several files" is single-commit shaped no matter how many edits it takes
- 2026-07-31: post-facto trapezoid experiment (0.23.0)
  - a published linear cycle was reshaped in place into the merge non-ff form with one
    `jj rebase -s` (close-out becomes the merge, rungs become the side leg, descendants
    follow); chids and ochid trailers survived, the bot repo needed nothing, and the one
    casualty was the close-out's recorded SHA, re-recorded per the backfill timing rule
  - details in chores-05.md "Post-facto trapezoid rewrite (2026-07-31)"; family-relevant if
    other repos want to adopt the trapezoid shape retroactively
  - the pre-restructure AGENTS.md is replaced (preserved in jj history, and verbatim as the
    template's AGENTS-iiac-perf.md)
  - the parked `punctuation-sweep` branch (TODO.md Todo #2) edited the old AGENTS.md; its
    AGENTS.md hunks are obsolete now that the typeable-punctuation rule ships as hard rule 8
    and prose.md, so the branch needs re-scoping to its README / TODO.md /
    notes/cycle-protocol.md conversions before landing
  - remaining pre-restructure local deltas (e.g. clap `verbatim_doc_comment` guidance) still
    need distilling into this file or proposing into the template; review findings recorded
    in the template's AGENTS-vc-x1-f5-20260730-review-iiac-perf-f5-20260731.md

   2026-08-01; process details to settle before first use)

     needed a coordinated force-push only because cycles push
     `main` directly

699	    origin: std::time::Instant,
700	    probes: &mut Vec<ProbeSummary>,
701	    settle_time_s: f64,
702	) {

704	        let gap_start = std::time::Instant::now();
705	        while gap_start.elapsed().as_secs_f64() < PROCESS_WARM_PROBE_GAP_S {
706	            for _ in 0..PROCESS_WARM_STEP_CHUNK {

708	            }

content.text:
The three warms and their code:

1. **Per-run warmup** — `warmup_and_probe` (harness.rs:740): the fixed `WARMUP = 10_000` steps, run in 16 chunks with a micro-probe after each. ~15 lines. This is the one the Todo replaces.
2. **Process warm** — `process_warm` (harness.rs:696): step the bench until `--settle-time` elapses, probing every 10 ms. ~15 lines plus the `claim_process_warm` once-flag.
3. **Block warm** — four inline lines in `run_blocked` (harness.rs:469-472): spin `bench.step()` for 2 ms after each sleep. No probes, no grading.

How much is shared: **#1 and #2 are already effectively one thing** — `process_warm` is called from *inside* `warmup_and_probe`, appends to the same probe vector, uses the same `Prober` and the same time origin, so they're two phases of a single probe series (that's exactly why the settle-time computation can span both). What differs is only the loop policy: #1 terminates on a step count in fixed chunks, #2 on elapsed time with time-gapped probes. **#3 shares nothing but the `bench.step()` primitive** — it's deliberately blind (a 2 ms ramp absorber with no instrumentation), and at 4 lines there's barely anything *to* share.

The interesting consequence for the Dynamic warmup Todo: warm-until-stable dissolves the remaining difference between #1 and #2. Both become "step the bench, probe periodically, stop when a condition holds" — the conditions being "trailing window reads A (or cap)" vs "settle-time budget spent". That's one mechanism with two exit policies, and the natural implementation is a single warm loop parameterized by its exit condition — at which point even the block warm is arguably the same loop with a fixed 2 ms policy and probing disabled. So the honest count today is "two and a half warms, two of them already fused"; after the Todo lands it should be one mechanism with three policies.

Which also settles the naming question: "Dynamic warmup" (singular, no "startup") ages *better*, because the entry's scope is really "the warmup mechanism becomes condition-driven", not just the startup instance. Want me to apply the rename with the cross-reference sweep (the "Qualify the environment" entry cites the old title, and harness.rs has two doc-comment mentions of `"Dynamic startup warmup" Todo` at lines 66 and 733)?

Ok, let's talk about blocks/batches the goal here is primarily a micro benchmark,
although communicating between threads would not typically be considered "micro"
but architecturally, for me, it is a fundamental and I want to squeeze every single
cycle out of it.

As a side note this has told me "placement" of the communicating threads is probably
the most important important factor.

content.text:
This reframing — "micro in the cycles-count sense, even though two threads are involved" — is exactly right, and the session's data both supports your side note and sharpens what blocks/batches need to become for that goal.

**Your placement conclusion is quantitatively overwhelming.** The tiers came out 35 / 133 / 633 ns — a 4× penalty for leaving the core, another 4.8× for leaving the L3, 18× end to end. Meanwhile *within* a tier, the trimmed stdev was 1.8-7 ns and run-to-run agreement ~1%. So placement is worth 4-18×, frequency is worth ~1.2×, and everything else you might optimize lives inside a few percent. The lever ordering is unambiguous: placement, then clock, then code. For a zc-ring-x1 user, "which cores do the two threads share" matters more than anything you can do to the ring's code — which is why the topology Todo (profiles, lCPU terminology, topology-aware Setup line) is really a *measurement prerequisite* for the cycle-squeezing program, not a nicety.

**What "squeeze every cycle" demands of the harness — and mostly already has:** the workflow is pin the tier (`--pin smt`/`llc`), pin the frequency (so ns = cycles), run `--blocks`, and compare against the LSC. The resolving power is already there: the SMT run's CI95 was ±0.025 ns — a tenth of a cycle. One cycle at 3.77 GHz is 0.265 ns, so in the SMT and cross-CCD configs (LSC 0.03-0.55 ns) you can *already* detect a single-cycle improvement from one pair of 30 s runs. The same-CCX and cross-CCX runs had LSC ~2.1-2.3 ns ≈ 8 cycles — there you'd need more blocks or longer runs to resolve one cycle, but that's a knob, not a wall.

**Where blocks/batches fall short for this goal: placement is currently *controlled or invisible*, never *measured*.** Unpinned, the scheduler's choice smears the distribution across tiers, blocks re-roll it (that's how we found the SMT fast mode — by accident), and the CI honestly reports the variance of a mixture — a deployment statistic, not a code metric. The missing feature is cheap and fits the existing architecture: sample each bench thread's CPU (`sched_getcpu` is a vDSO call, ~10 ns) at batch seams, classify the pair against the discovered topology (same core / same LLC / cross-LLC), and then:

- **batches** gain a placement label → migrations become *attributed* steps ("step 280% @4.1s: cross-LLC → SMT") instead of anonymous ones, the same way the env grade attributed DVFS;
- **blocks** gain per-tier stratification → an unpinned `--blocks` run reports per-placement-class means instead of one smeared CI, turning the scheduler's wandering from noise into a free stratified experiment.

That's a natural extension bullet for the topology Todo — placement tracking is the measurement side of the same feature whose control side is the pin profiles.

One caveat to keep in the record: for cycle-squeezing on *this* bench family, `inner` batching hides per-op variation (each sample is 4-23 round trips averaged), so the mode you're optimizing is the *sustained* per-op cost, not the isolated-op cost. That's usually the right target for a ring — but it's a choice, and `-i 1` is the escape hatch when it isn't.

The plain version: your data says where the two threads sit dwarfs everything else — 4× to 18× — so the harness's most important job for this goal is controlling and reporting placement. The machinery to detect single-cycle code improvements already exists (pin placement, pin frequency, use blocks, trust the LSC); the missing piece is having the harness *observe* placement when it isn't pinned, per batch and per block, so nothing about where threads ran is ever anonymous. Want me to fold the placement-tracking design into the topology Todo?

message.content: That would be good, but a bench doesn't have to inform us if creates threads or sub-processes so I don't think it can absolutely know, or maybe it can if there the kernel can tell us?

content.text:
The kernel can tell us — not absolutely, but observationally, and that turns out to be enough. The mechanism:

- **Thread enumeration without cooperation**: `/proc/self/task/` lists every thread of the process, whether or not the bench announced it. Per thread, `/proc/self/task/<tid>/stat` gives the CPU it last ran on (field 39) plus its accumulated CPU time. Sub-processes are reachable the same way via `/proc/self/task/<tid>/children`, recursively. All unprivileged, and it's exactly how `ps -L`/`htop` do it.
- **Filtering who matters**: the harness doesn't need the bench to say which threads communicate — CPU-time *deltas* between two sweeps identify them. A spinning worker accumulates ~100% of a seam interval; a parked helper accumulates ~0. The active set falls out of arithmetic.
- **The measuring thread itself**: `sched_getcpu()` is a vDSO call (~10 ns), exact and essentially free at every seam.

The honesty caveats, which are real but bounded:

1. **It's sampled truth, not a complete record.** A sweep at each batch seam yields a placement timeline at 15-50 ms resolution; a migration inside a batch is invisible until the next seam, and a thread born and dead entirely between seams is never seen. But the consumer of this data is attribution — "did the step at 4.1s coincide with a placement change" — and the step detector works at batch granularity anyway, so the sampling matches the resolution of the thing it explains.
2. **"Last ran on" is where the scheduler last put it**, which for a spinning thread equals where it runs; for an idle thread it's stale — but idle threads are exactly the ones the CPU-time filter drops.

Cost: a readdir plus a handful of small `stat` reads per seam, single-digit microseconds against a seam that already costs 1-2 ms. Negligible, and it can degrade to per-block if a bench ever has hundreds of threads.

So the design is two-tier: **cooperative knowledge** (threads pinned through the pool are known exactly) layered over **observational knowledge** (the /proc sweep sees everything, sampled) — and the report states which tier a claim comes from. Folding it into the topology Todo now:

- `--pin` help/README say slots are logical CPU ids
7. Topology-aware pinning and lCPU terminology: discover the
   CPU sharing tree at runtime and describe every pin by the
   nearest shared level, not "unique CPUs". Evidence: the
   2026-08-01 pinning experiment (`zcr-with-2t -d 30 --blocks 5`
   on the 3900X, boost on) measured the round trip at ~35 ns on
   SMT siblings (shared L1/L2), ~133 ns same-CCX (shared L3),
   ~633 ns cross-CCX (shared fabric only); cross-CCX vs
   cross-CCD differed by 1.6 ns against a ~2 ns LSC, so the L3
   boundary is the only fabric tier that matters on Zen 2, and
   the unpinned scheduler's ~127-135 ns core mass matches
   same-CCX placement
   - standardize terms by shared resource, vendor structures as
     examples only: **lCPU** (kernel-schedulable execution
     context, the `--pin` unit), **core** (lCPUs sharing L1 and
     the execution engine), **cluster** (cores sharing a
     mid-level cache: Intel E-core module, ARM DynamIQ; absent
     on AMD), **LLC domain** (cores sharing last-level cache:
     AMD CCX), **package** (LLC domains sharing on-package
     fabric), **NUMA node**. Levels a machine lacks collapse
     out; the tree may be asymmetric (hybrid parts have levels
     only on some branches); matches the kernel sched-domain
     ladder SMT/CLS/MC/PKG/NUMA
   - core *type* (big.LITTLE, P/E cores) is an attribute of a
     core, not a level: cluster identical (part id, capacity,
     max freq) cores into classes and report the classes; read
     `cpu_capacity` (ARM/RISC-V arch_topology),
     `/sys/devices/cpu_core/cpus` + `/sys/devices/cpu_atom/cpus`
     (Intel hybrid), part id + `cpuinfo_max_freq` as fallback;
     avoid the big/LITTLE branding (DynamIQ ships 3-4 tiers)
   - discovery is unprivileged sysfs: partition lCPUs by
     `cache/index*/shared_cpu_list` per cache level, plus
     `topology/{thread_siblings,cluster_cpus}_list`,
     `physical_package_id`, `/sys/devices/system/node`;
     cacheinfo is populated on x86_64 and arm64, patchy on
     RISC-V, so fall back to topology files and mark cache
     levels unknown
   - the Setup `bench pin` line reports the pool's partition and
     nearest shared level, e.g. `[0, 12] (2 slots, 2 lCPUs on
     1 core - shared L1/L2)`; retires bare "CPU" from all output
   - auto profiles derived from the discovered tree (`--pin
     smt`, `--pin llc`, `--pin xllc`) so one command line is
     portable across boxes; extends the config `[profiles]`
     mechanism `--pin` already resolves

content.text:
The placement-tracking design is folded into the topology Todo (#7) as its own bullet block, and the list validates clean. The key points now on record:

- **Two tiers of knowledge**, with the report always saying which one a claim comes from: *cooperative* (threads placed through the `--pin` pool — exact) and *observational* (the `/proc/self/task/` sweep at batch seams — complete coverage of threads and sub-processes the bench never announced, but sampled at seam cadence).
- **The kernel answers your question affirmatively**: last-ran lCPU from each task's `stat`, children recursively via `/children`, active-thread identification by CPU-time deltas — no bench cooperation needed, no privileges, ~microseconds per seam.
- **The honest limit is sampling, and it's matched to its consumer**: migrations inside a batch are unseen, but the step detector that placement labels would explain also works at batch granularity, so the observation resolution equals the attribution resolution.
- **The two payoffs**: batches get placement-class labels (attributed steps, like the DVFS attribution the env grade already does), and unpinned `--blocks` runs stratify by placement class instead of smearing — formalizing the accident that revealed the SMT fast mode.

So the absolute-knowledge answer is: no, the harness can't have a complete event-level record without cooperation (that would take perf/eBPF tracepoints and privileges) — but it can have sampled, unprivileged, cooperation-free truth at exactly the granularity its detectors operate at, which is what attribution needs. All still uncommitted in the working copy, riding with the rest.
